records.sourceFile: A cherry tree ripe for picking - The relationship between the acute-chronic workload ratio and health problems.pdf

paper.citation: Dalen-Lorentsen T, Andersen TE, Bjørneboe J, Vagle M, Martin KN, Kleppen M, et al. A cherry tree ripe for picking: The relationship between the acute:chronic workload ratio and health problems. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2021.
paper.abstract: Objective: To investigate whether the relationship between the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and health problems varies when different methodological approaches are used. Design: Prospective cohort study. Methods: An online questionnaire collected daily health and training data from 86 elite youth footballers for 105 days. ACWR was calculated with 21- and 28-day chronic periods, coupled and uncoupled, exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) and rolling average, and categorized by pre-defined bins and z-scores; three outcomes were tested in 108 random-effects logistic regression analyses. Results: 6250 training days and 196 health problems were recorded; 24 (22%) of 108 analyses were significant. Conclusions: The relationship between ACWR and health problems depends on methodological choices.
paper.tldr: In 86 elite youth footballers, roughly one in five of 108 ACWR analysis variants showed a significant link to health problems, and the result depended on how ACWR was calculated and analysed. Treat any single reported ACWR association with caution.
paper.methods: A prospective cohort of six elite U-19 Norwegian football teams (three girls' and three boys') ran from July to October 2017, covering summer break and 13 to 14 weeks of in-season competition. Players reported daily session duration and RPE by online questionnaire (training load in arbitrary units = duration times RPE) and new or worsening health problems, which a clinician then classified using UEFA guidelines by telephone interview. Twelve ACWR variants were tested against three outcomes (all health problems, all injuries, new non-contact injuries), giving 108 random-effects logistic regression analyses that were not adjusted for sex, age or clustering (adjusted analyses are in a supplement).
paper.findings: The text reports 24 of 108 analyses (22%) as significant, but the counts in Table 2 and the forest plots sum to 22 (about 20%). Significance was most frequent with EWMA (15 of 36, 42%) and in low-versus-high comparisons (12 of 36, 33%), and rare for medium-versus-low (2 of 36) and new non-contact injuries (2 of 36). The largest odds ratio was about 5.3 (95% CI 1.83 to 15.2), low versus high ACWR for all injuries, which the text and Table 2 place under coupled 7:21 EWMA with pre-defined bins, although the figure labels that row differently.
paper.limitations: Health problems were self-reported and not medically confirmed, 88 of 196 were not classified, 31% of daily questionnaires were unanswered, and in the post-study survey (53% response) 29% admitted not reporting all health problems. The Discussion and Table 2 disagree on several figures, including new non-contact injuries (2% vs 6%) and 28-day vs 21-day periods (text says 28 days had more significant results, the table shows 15% vs 26%), and the figure's ACWR labels do not match Table 2; table values are reported here. The PDF prints no publication year (a '${year}' placeholder), so 2020 comes from the Crossref record.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff reading ACWR studies should ask whether all analyses were reported and how ACWR was calculated before trusting a single significant result. When collecting data for youth squads, the authors argue for recording all health complaints, not only time-loss injuries, but the paper does not support using ACWR thresholds to manage load.
paper.athleteDev: Limited. The study does not test whether ACWR-guided load changes improve performance. Its relevance is that calculation choices (period length, rolling average vs EWMA, categories) change the reported load-health picture, so ACWR bands should not be used as fixed training prescriptions.
paper.rtp: Not applicable as a return-to-sport study. It reports health problems across a season, not return-to-play decisions, so it cannot be used to decide how quickly a returning player can increase training load.

records.sourceFile: A Review of the Validity and Reliability of Accelerometer-Based Metrics From Upper Back–Mounted GNSS Player Tracking Systems for Athlete Training Load Monitoring.pdf

paper.citation: Dawson L, Beato M, Devereux G, McErlain-Naylor SA. A Review of the Validity and Reliability of Accelerometer-Based Metrics From Upper Back-Mounted GNSS Player Tracking Systems for Athlete Training Load Monitoring. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(8):e460-e475.
paper.abstract: Athlete load monitoring with upper back-mounted GNSS player tracking is common in team sports, and accelerometer-based metrics may add information that GNSS alone cannot provide. This review appraises the validity and reliability of these accelerometers and their metrics (for example PlayerLoad, Dynamic Stress Load and Body Load). Reliability depends on equipment model, signal processing and activity. Upper back placement may be suboptimal for estimating mechanical load. Validity has mostly been judged against other load and intensity measures, with correlations that vary in size and certainty. Metrics should not be compared between athletes or manufacturers, and further study is needed on links to biomechanical load pathways.
paper.tldr: Upper back-mounted GNSS accelerometer metrics are generally reliable within the same device, but their validity depends on filtering, device and activity. Do not compare them between athletes or manufacturers.
paper.methods: A narrative review of accelerometer-based metrics from upper back-mounted GNSS units in team sports. The authors describe the published equations for PlayerLoad, Body Load (including the New Body Load variant) and Dynamic Stress Load, then tabulate validity studies against motion capture and ground reaction force (raw and filtered data) and reliability studies (CV and ICC). The paper describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria.
paper.findings: Reliability of GNSS-housed raw accelerometer data is largely high to very high with mostly good CVs, but metric reliability varied (PlayerLoad CVs of 14.5% to 24.5% in one soccer task study), and raw signals are generally less valid than filtered ones. PlayerLoad correlated highly to very highly with distance (r = 0.70 to 0.98), whereas Dynamic Stress Load showed no correlation with distance per minute in one futsal study; metrics correlated moderately to very highly with heart rate but only low or negligibly with blood lactate. In rugby league, a 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation was associated with injury probability (AUC 0.585, 95% CI 0.482 to 0.672, p = 0.048), while 2- and 3-week accumulations were not, and other studies linked both higher and lower values to injury.
paper.limitations: The review describes no search method or inclusion criteria, so study selection cannot be judged. The authors note that validity depends on manufacturer, processing, filtering and activity, that vertical acceleration can mask collision accelerations in rugby, and that links to internal biomechanical load are rarely studied. Upper back placement may be suboptimal for estimating whole-body mechanical load, and the printed confidence interval for the injury AUC (0.482 to 0.672) includes 0.5.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the same device for repeated comparisons and avoid comparing athletes or manufacturers directly; the authors suggest low-pass filtering near 20 Hz for high-impact and 10 Hz for lower-impact activities, using reported CVs to set the size of a meaningful change, and tight sensor fixation. For rugby collisions, a 2D Body Load corrected the vertical-masking problem, but PlayerLoadSlow gave mixed results, so neither should be treated as settled, and none of these metrics should be treated as a measure of tissue load or injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports within-device, within-athlete trend monitoring of acceleration load across training, including sprint and change-of-direction demands, because PlayerLoad rose with running speed and with more direction changes. It does not support comparing athletes or manufacturers, and it does not show that any metric guides training design.
paper.rtp: Limited. The review reports one rugby league association between a 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation and injury probability (AUC 0.585), and notes that both increased and decreased values have been linked to injury risk. It cannot be used to set return-to-play load thresholds or judge tissue readiness.

records.sourceFile: A systematic review and meta-analysis of wearable satellite system technology for liner sprint profiling - Technological innovations and practical applications.pdf

paper.citation: Cormier P, Meylan C, Agar-Newman D, Geneau D, Epp-Stobbe A, Lenetsky S, et al. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Wearable Satellite System Technology for Linear Sprint Profiling: Technological Innovations and Practical Applications. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2023.
paper.abstract: An emerging practice is the use of GNSS technology to profile team-sports athletes in training and competition. This narrative systematic review with meta-analysis evaluated satellite sensor usage for sprint modeling and its validity and reliability. Sixteen studies were retained from 1,485 identified. Effects were expressed as standardized mean differences between GNSS-derived and criterion (radar and laser) values for maximal sprint speed, acceleration constant, maximal theoretical velocity, relative force and relative power; all were small. No publication bias was found, sampling rate and sensor manufacturer moderated results, and heterogeneity was moderate to high. The authors conclude that all-out linear sprints with GNSS can be integrated into sessions when robust and consistent processing is used.
paper.tldr: GNSS sprint modeling shows small pooled differences from radar or laser for top-speed metrics, but the acceleration metrics tau and F0 are less reliable. Use devices sampling at 10 Hz or more, report processing steps, and treat acceleration metrics with caution.
paper.methods: Following PRISMA, the authors searched PubMed and SPORTDiscus up to 1 July 2023 using GNSS, GPS, accelerometer and IMU terms with sprinting, team sports and athletes, plus reference lists. Eligible studies were concurrent validity or reliability studies of GNSS linear sprint outputs in athletes, in English and peer reviewed; the protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework. Study quality used a modified Downs and Black checklist, and a mixed-effects meta-analysis of radar or laser criterion studies pooled SMDs, with moderator analyses for sampling rate (10 Hz or more vs under 10 Hz) and manufacturer.
paper.findings: Sixteen studies were included; criteria were radar or laser in 7, timing gates in 5, and video or a sliding platform in the rest, and funnel plots and Egger tests showed no publication bias. Pooled SMDs were small for maximal sprint speed (d = 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.42, I2 = 55%), tau (d = -0.18, 95% CI -0.60 to 0.23, I2 = 87%), V0 (d = 0.14), relative F0 (d = 0.15) and relative Pmax (d = 0.21). For speed, devices at 10 Hz or more showed no clear bias (MSS d = 0.11, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.26), while SPI at 5 Hz (d = 0.75) and SensorEverywhere at 16 Hz (d = 0.59) overestimated it; intertrial CVs were under 5% for MSS, V0 and relative Pmax but over 5% for F0 and tau.
paper.limitations: The meta-analysis includes only radar and laser criteria, and many studies used small samples, filtered or raw data inconsistently, and under-reported filter settings (only 2 GNSS studies reported full filter specifications). Several included studies used timing gates as the criterion, which the authors say overestimate acceleration-phase metrics and may not suit validity studies, and only two databases were searched. The year 2023 is as printed in the PDF; the Crossref record gives 2024, so the PDF year is used.
paper.practicalImplications: Sprint profiling with GNSS is reasonable for top-speed metrics when the device samples at 10 Hz or more and the same device and processing are used across sessions. Staff should not rely on GNSS tau or F0 as precise measures of acceleration capacity, and should record the sampling rate, filtering, onset and end-of-sprint rules, and satellite quality with every profile.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports using standardized all-out linear sprints within training to build force-velocity profiles and track changes in top speed, with best use when the same device and processing are used across time. It does not show that acceleration-based profile metrics detect small training changes reliably.
paper.rtp: Limited. The review covers healthy trained athletes and does not test sprint profiles after injury. Its suggested rehabilitation use is a general concept, so it cannot be used to set sprint-based return-to-sport criteria or judge readiness from acceleration metrics.

records.sourceFile: Focused review of sleep wearable technology and its application in sports performance.pdf

paper.citation: Kaufman MW, Shetty M, Nguyen C, Abas J, Fredericson M, Zeitzer J. Focused Review of Sleep Wearable Technology and Its Application in Sports Performance. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2025;24(6):171-176.
paper.abstract: The authors review the history, accuracy and current use of sleep wearables, which are mostly wrist-worn actigraphs. They conclude that wearables detect sleep reasonably well but struggle to separate quiet wakefulness from early sleep, and that proprietary sleep scores are not yet clinically interpretable for athletes.
paper.tldr: Sleep wearables can show sleep trends across a season, but their summary scores have not been linked to training, performance or recovery. When the device and the athlete's own sense of sleep disagree, the athlete's report should take priority.
paper.methods: Narrative review of published actigraphy validation studies and athlete sleep studies. The authors state the review is more narrative than structured because device validity depends on hardware and software that can change.
paper.findings: Wearables show high sensitivity for detecting sleep but poor sensitivity for detecting wake, with wake accuracy of about 49% to 60% in validation studies. Actigraphy agreed with polysomnography at 81% to 90% in elite athletes in the cited work. No study has linked a consumer summary sleep score to training, performance or recovery outcomes.
paper.limitations: The authors acknowledge that the review is not structured, that many validation studies are industry sponsored, and that device algorithms are proprietary. The paper presents no original data.
paper.practicalImplications: Use wearables to see sleep trends across a season and around travel or schedule changes, but do not treat a summary sleep score as a clinical result. Keep clinical presentation and subjective report as the basis for decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: track sleep trends across a season, including travel, to see how schedule changes line up with training and recovery. Do not set sleep-score targets for athletes, since the score's link to performance is unestablished.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review suggests wearables may help detect sleep disturbances that can accompany concussion, but it states they are likely not sensitive or specific and are not a substitute for clinical presentation. Clinical examination and the athlete's report should guide decisions.

records.sourceFile: Height restrictions for dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry - What are our options for body composition and bone health precision.pdf

paper.citation: Redinger AL, Russell JL, Allen SMF, Baker BS. Height Restrictions for Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry: What Are Our Options for Body Composition and Bone Health Precision? Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024.
paper.abstract: Sixty adults were scanned three times on GE Lunar Prodigy or Hologic Horizon A DXA units, and a combined upper and lower body region of interest was built from a flipped scan. The combined scan added less than 1% error on the Lunar Prodigy but added large bone mineral content error on the newer Hologic and GE units.
paper.tldr: On older GE Lunar Prodigy systems, a combined-region scan keeps body composition precise for athletes who exceed the table height, with less than 1% added error. On newer Hologic and GE units, the combined method makes bone mineral content too unreliable for serial comparison, so use the same landmarks and region heights.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional precision study. Participants completed two identical total-body scans and one flipped total-body scan, analysed by trained technicians using ISCD guidance. Coefficient of variation, paired t tests, Cohen d, Pearson r and Bland-Altman analysis compared baseline scans with the combined-region scans.
paper.findings: On the Lunar Prodigy, the combined-region scan changed precision by 0.25% (bone-free lean mass) to 0.63% (fat mass), with a significant but trivial bone mineral content difference (p = 0.002, d = 0.10). On the Hologic Horizon A, bone mineral content error rose by 4.35% (CV 0.80% to 5.15%), fat mass by 0.31% and bone-free lean mass by less than 0.01%; the BMC and fat mass differences were significant but with trivial effect sizes. On the iDXA, the authors report 3.71% bone mineral content, 4.80% lean mass and 7.39% fat mass error from a single participant.
paper.limitations: The participants were non-athletes who fit on the table, and the iDXA result is from one person. The analysis comes from one lab with trained technicians, and the study does not test athletes above the table height limit directly.
paper.practicalImplications: Labs with older Lunar Prodigy units can use the combined-region method for serial assessment of tall athletes, after checking baseline precision. Labs with newer Hologic or GE units should instead use the shortest common region of interest across all scans and keep the same bony landmarks, because the combined method adds large bone error.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: athletes taller than the table limit (about 193 cm) can be tracked with the combined-region scan on an older Lunar Prodigy, or with the shortest common region on newer units, as long as the same landmarks and region heights are used over time. Do not compare body composition across scans that cut different body segments.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study does not address return to sport. Bone-mineral trends from scans with altered or omitted regions should not be used to judge bone recovery or injury risk in tall athletes.

records.sourceFile: PEP - A tackle value measuring the prevention of expected points.pdf

paper.citation: Bajons R, Koslik JO, Michels R, Ötting M. PEP: a tackle value measuring the prevention of expected points. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.08508v1. 2024.
paper.abstract: The authors develop a metric, prevented expected points (PEP), that values each tackle in American football by comparing the actual end-of-play yard line with a predicted yard line for a hypothetical missed tackle. They use high-resolution tracking data, a random forest for the yard-line distribution, and expected points values, and then fit a mixed-effects model to relate tackle values to individual tacklers. The authors present the approach as a way to assess defensive performance beyond tackle counts.
paper.tldr: A tackle-value metric built from NFL tracking data that estimates expected points prevented by each tackle. It offers a more context-aware view of defensive tackling than tackle counts, but it is not validated against outcomes and has known biases on pass plays.
paper.methods: Used NFL Big Data Bowl 2024 data (first nine weeks of the 2022 season, 10 Hz tracking, play-by-play and tackle records). Plays with penalties were excluded, leaving 11,313 tackles. A random forest estimated the conditional distribution of the end-of-play yard line, expected points came from an XGBoost model trained on 2011-2021 play-by-play data, and PEP was the difference between expected points for the hypothetical and observed plays. A GAMLSS mixed-effects model with random effects for tackler, ball carrier and offensive team was fitted to the PEP values, with uncertainty estimated by bootstrapping full drives.
paper.findings: The yard-line prediction had an average RMSE of 5.74 and MAE of 3.13, and the expected points model had an MAE of 3.6391 on the 2022 season, matching a comparison model (3.6395). In the mixed-effects ranking, the highest median tackler effects were Dexter Lawrence (DT, 0.115) and Damarri Mathis (CB, 0.114), and the top three players on the 2022 NFL tackles leaderboard (all inside linebackers) were in the top ten inside linebackers by this measure. Cumulative PEP favored linebackers and safeties, while average PEP favored defensive backs. In a run-play-only analysis of 5,889 tackles, Jeff Okudah (CB) ranked first, and adding 1,669 missed tackles changed tacklers' effects only modestly (r = 0.88).
paper.limitations: The metric uses one half-season of tracking data, and the authors describe the rankings as sensible but not validated against outcomes. Passing plays may bias results toward cornerbacks who allow catches, and missed tackles are left out of the main analysis because the sample of 1,669 was judged too small. The PDF is the arXiv preprint (July 2024), not the published version, and it may differ from the journal article. Its year is 2024, which differs from the crossrefYear in the batch input (2026); the PDF year is kept. The journal record was not compared with the PDF text beyond title and authors.
paper.practicalImplications: Defensive reviews can add game-situation tackle value to tackle counts, so that tackles in high-stakes moments are weighted more heavily, as the authors suggest for player evaluation and scouting. Cornerback and other defensive back values should be read with caution because of the pass-play bias. Use the bootstrap ranges for each tackler rather than a single rank, since the authors note that top players had narrower distributions and that players with few tackles are pulled toward the average.
paper.athleteDev: Use game-situation tackle value, alongside tackle counts, when reviewing defensive performance. Give extra caution to defensive back values, which the authors say may reflect coverage on pass plays rather than tackling ability.
paper.rtp: The study covers regular-season tackling by healthy players and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot be used for return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Percentile rankings and position differences for absolute and allometrically scaled performance measures from the NFL Scouting Combine.pdf

paper.citation: Gillen ZM. Percentile Rankings and Position Differences for Absolute and Allometrically Scaled Performance Measures From the National Football League Scouting Combine. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2023.
paper.abstract: This study provides percentile rankings for absolute and allometrically scaled NFL Scouting Combine measures in 3,015 players from 2015 to 2019, both overall and by position group. It also tests whether allometric scaling changes position-specific differences. The author provides the allometric parameters so that coaches and practitioners can scale combine data themselves.
paper.tldr: Updated NFL Scouting Combine percentile norms for 40-yd, split, jump, agility and bench press tests, both raw and body-mass-scaled. Position differences shift once allometric scaling is applied, so both views are useful for comparing players.
paper.methods: Combine data from 2015 to 2019 for 3,015 players, excluding 2020 to 2022 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Players were grouped into eight position groups, and percentile ranks, means and SDs were calculated for absolute and allometrically scaled measures. Polynomial regression tested the best model of body mass against each measure, correlations were compared before and after scaling, and one-way ANOVA tested position differences. Quarterback bench press data (8 players) were excluded.
paper.findings: Body mass was moderately to highly correlated with absolute measures (|r| of at least 0.638, p under 0.001), but was negligibly related to all allometrically scaled measures (|r| of 0.031 or less), except bench press (r = -0.053, p = 0.008). Position groups differed significantly for absolute measures, with DB and WR faster and jumping higher and farther than LB, QB, RB and TE, and linemen stronger on the bench press. After scaling, DL, LB, RB and TE tended to outperform DB and WR, and QB and OL had the poorest performance. Polynomial regression showed no consistent best model of body mass, and only the 10-yd split and L-cone were best described as linear.
paper.limitations: The norms are limited to combine invitees from 2015 to 2019 and do not cover 2020 to 2022. Quarterback bench press data were too few (8 players) to analyse. Body composition was not measured, so the explanations for position differences rest on other studies. The author notes that combine scores are not always a good indicator of playing potential, and the study does not test whether combine measures predict NFL performance or draft outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and practitioners can compare a combine athlete against the percentile tables, and can use the allometric parameters to scale their own data. Use scaled values when comparing players of different body masses and positions, since raw results can mainly reflect body mass, and keep in mind that the best scaling approach varies by test. The author suggests these norms can guide position-specific strength and conditioning planning.
paper.athleteDev: Use the percentile tables and allometric parameters as normative benchmarks for testing and for comparing athletes of different body mass, for example to judge jump or sprint results relative to body size. Position profiles differ by method: linemen do the most absolute bench press repetitions and skill players have the fastest raw split times, but after scaling RB and LB lead the bench press and OL and WR are lowest, so check both views before setting training priorities.
paper.rtp: The study describes healthy combine participants at a single time point and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot be used to judge whether an injured athlete is ready to return or to set return-to-play benchmarks.

records.sourceFile: Position-Specific Differences in Speed Profiles Among National Football League Scouting Combine Participants.pdf

paper.citation: Gillen ZM. Position-Specific Differences in Speed Profiles Among National Football League Scouting Combine Participants. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024.
paper.abstract: The study examined speed profiles (vmax, t and amax) calculated from the 40-yard dash and its splits in 2,156 NFL Scouting Combine participants across eight position groups. Skill positions had the greatest vmax and amax and lowest t, while offensive linemen had the lowest vmax and amax and highest t. Speed profile variables were related to other combine measures, with the weakest relationships found for offensive linemen.
paper.tldr: Speed profile values from the NFL Combine differ clearly by position, with defensive backs and wide receivers fastest and offensive linemen slowest. Calculating vmax, t and amax from the 40-yard dash splits may add information beyond raw times.
paper.methods: Data came from NFL Scouting Combines in 2017, 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2023, with COVID-affected 2020 and 2021 excluded. Speed profile variables were calculated from 10-, 20- and 40-yard split times, and the author used one-way ANOVA and Pearson correlations with height, body mass, bench press, jump, pro-agility and L-cone tests.
paper.findings: Defensive backs and wide receivers had the highest vmax (9.33 and 9.34 m/s) and amax and the lowest t, while offensive linemen had the lowest vmax (8.00 m/s) and amax (11.44 m/s/s) and the highest t (0.69 s); running backs did not differ from defensive backs and wide receivers for t or amax. Across the whole sample, vmax, t and amax were significantly correlated with all combine tests, with t showing the weakest relationships.
paper.limitations: The PDF prints the year 2024 (NSCA copyright and journal header), while the Crossref record lists 2025; the PDF year is used here. The text does not state the participants' sex or playing level beyond NFL Scouting Combine participation, and the paper is a secondary analysis of publicly available data with no on-field speed measures. The author notes that position-specific adaptation and genetic selection could not be separated.
paper.practicalImplications: Calculating vmax, t and amax from the 40-yard dash and splits can add information beyond raw times, and coaches can use position-level profiles to decide whether to prioritise maximal speed, acceleration or both. Because the study reports only group averages and correlations, these profiles should be compared with a player's own data rather than applied as fixed targets.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The position means for vmax, t and amax (Table 1) can serve as reference values when an athlete's own 10-, 20- and 40-yard splits are converted to a speed profile. The author suggests training both maximal speed and acceleration rather than only short accelerations for linemen, but this was not tested.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It contains no injured players, no return-to-play testing and no follow-up of sprint mechanics after injury, so the speed profiles should not be used to judge readiness to return.

records.sourceFile: Practitioner usage, applications, and understanding of wearable GPS and accelerometer technology in team sports.pdf

paper.citation: Dawson L, McErlain-Naylor SA, Devereux G, Beato M. Practitioner Usage, Applications, and Understanding of Wearable GPS and Accelerometer Technology in Team Sports. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024.
paper.abstract: The survey investigated how 72 practitioners in team sports use, apply and understand trunk-mounted GPS and accelerometer technology for athlete load monitoring. Practitioners widely supported GPS, and most used wearable data to inform training, but fewer used it for competition decisions. Accelerometer-derived metrics were used less and understood less well than GPS metrics, and practitioners asked for more standardization and education.
paper.tldr: Most team sport practitioners in this survey use wearable data to plan training, but far fewer use it for match decisions. Accelerometer-derived metrics are less well understood than GPS metrics, so staff should check what each metric measures before acting on it.
paper.methods: A cross-sectional online survey, distributed through social networking, sport science and coaching networks, and online noticeboards from May 2021 to May 2022, asked 72 practitioners with regular GPS and accelerometer load monitoring experience about usage, applications and understanding, using Likert, rating and open questions. Open responses were analysed with six-phase thematic analysis, and two researchers independently categorised the quality of respondents' metric definitions.
paper.findings: All 72 respondents supported GPS use in their sport, and 70.8% agreed it is important for success. 87.5% agreed that wearable data informs training prescription, but only 50% agreed it influences decisions in competition. Total distance was the most common metric (93%), 84.7% found GPS metrics easy to understand compared with 47.2% for accelerometer-derived metrics, and self-rated understanding was similar regardless of how accurate respondents' definitions were.
paper.limitations: The sample is self-selected, so response bias is likely, and respondents could select several sports, levels and roles, so these could not be compared. Reported use of accelerometer load metrics was inconsistent within the survey (39% in one question, 56% in a later one), and only 38 respondents gave a definition. Questions were not compulsory and the completion rate cannot be calculated.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should confirm what accelerometer-derived metrics measure before using them to prescribe training, since several practitioners rated their understanding at 6 or 7 of 10 but gave poor or incorrect definitions. The authors, citing earlier work, advise using the same unit for each player and consistent garments before comparing sessions.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Before a practitioner uses an accelerometer-derived load metric to plan sessions, they should confirm how the metric is calculated, because respondents named 'black box' algorithms and different brand formulas as concerns. Each player should wear the same unit, as the authors note this reduces interunit variation when sessions are compared.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It surveys practitioners about training load monitoring and reports no injured players, rehabilitation outcomes or return-to-play decisions. Respondents said accelerometer data informed injury rehabilitation (median 6 of 10), but the survey does not test whether these data guide return to play.

records.sourceFile: Predicting sprint performance from the vertical and horizontal jumps in National Football League Combine athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Agar-Newman DJ, MacRae F, Tsai M-C, Klimstra M. Predicting Sprint Performance From the Vertical and Horizontal Jumps in National Football League Combine Athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(8):1433-1439.
paper.abstract: The authors built regression equations that predict sprint times over four segments of the NFL Combine 36.58-m sprint from vertical jump, broad jump, height and body mass. Models were developed on half of the data and tested on the other half. The equations explained 74 to 84% of the variance in segment times, with small biases and 5 to 6% of predictions outside the limits of agreement.
paper.tldr: Sprint times over the 36.58-m (40-yard) sprint and its splits can be estimated from jump tests and body size, which helps when a player did not sprint. The authors propose using the gap between predicted and actual times to flag areas to examine, but the estimates are not precise enough for exact individual times.
paper.methods: Retrospective NFL Combine data (1999 to 2020) from a public website were filtered to players with complete records. Backward stepwise multiple regression on a training set predicted the four sprint segments from vertical jump, broad jump, height and body mass, and Bland-Altman analysis compared predicted and measured times on a test set.
paper.findings: Adjusted R2 was 0.76 for 9.14-m time, 0.74 for 9.14 to 18.29-m time, 0.79 for 18.29 to 36.58-m time and 0.84 for 36.58-m time, with standard errors of the estimate of 0.04 to 0.12 s. Biases in the test set were -0.05, -0.04, -0.02 and -0.02 s, with RMSE of 0.07, 0.05, 0.07 and 0.12 s. Mass and broad jump had the largest standardized coefficients, and 5.0 to 5.8% of predictions in each segment lay outside the limits of agreement.
paper.limitations: The abstract and Subjects section give 4,149 players, Table 1 and the training and test split give 4,141, and the Statistical Analyses section gives 4,071 complete sets of data (from 7,171 or 7,174 downloaded), so the final sample size is not consistent. The NFL Combine uses a hand-trigger start and the Vertec may inflate jump height compared with force plate methods, as the authors note. The equations were fitted with stepwise regression on one split, and the authors caution against extrapolating beyond the performance levels studied.
paper.practicalImplications: The equations let staff estimate sprint times when a 36.58-m sprint was not run and compare an athlete's measured time with the predicted time. A player who runs faster or slower than predicted can prompt a look at technique or physical limits, but the 5 to 6% of predictions outside the agreement limits show that the estimates need checking against measured sprints.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Staff preparing players for the Combine can use vertical jump, broad jump and body mass to estimate each sprint segment and see where a player's sprint may be below or above what his jumps predict. A gap between predicted and measured sprint times is a reason to look at technique or force application, not a fixed training target.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It uses draft-eligible players tested at the Combine and reports no injured athletes, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes, so the prediction equations should not be used to judge readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Selecting Metrics That Matter - Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and I.pdf

paper.citation: Bishop C, Jordan M, Torres-Ronda L, Loturco I, Harry J, Virgile A, et al. Selecting Metrics That Matter: Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and Injury Rehabilitation Testing. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2023.
paper.abstract: The countermovement jump is widely used in strength and conditioning, but no overarching guidance exists on which metrics to choose for each purpose. This article discusses how the metrics chosen differ for performance profiling, neuromuscular fatigue monitoring and testing of injured athletes.
paper.tldr: Choose countermovement jump metrics by purpose: jump height, peak force and peak power for profiling, time-based metrics for fatigue monitoring, and asymmetry and landing force for rehabilitation. Before calling any change real, compare it with the test's coefficient of variation.
paper.methods: Narrative review, with no search method described. Sections cover the associations of CMJ metrics with strength, linear speed and change-of-direction ability, their sensitivity to neuromuscular fatigue, and their use with injured athletes. Table 1 summarizes acute and 19-week training effect sizes from one study of elite snowboard cross athletes, and Tables 2 and 3 apply the change-versus-CV method to example group and individual data.
paper.findings: Jump height, peak force and peak power correlate with strength, linear speed and change-of-direction measures, with correlations varying with whether absolute or relative values are used. A meta-analysis cited by the authors found maximal jump height and peak power were not sensitive to fatigue (ES -0.04 each), while other cited studies found flight time (ES -1.4) and relative net impulse (ES -0.69) changed most immediately after intense exercise, and time to peak power and flight time:contraction time ratio changed most over 24-72 h. In injured athletes the authors suggest landing force and asymmetry measures may be more useful than jump height or peak power.
paper.limitations: No search strategy is described, so the review cannot be checked for completeness. Several recommendations rest on the authors' anecdotal experience, and Tables 2 and 3 are worked examples of calculation (Table 2 is stated to be hypothetical) rather than observed data. The running header prints Volume 00 and Number 00, and the PDF gives no DOI or page numbers, so the citation omits them.
paper.practicalImplications: Select CMJ metrics by purpose: jump height, peak force and peak power for profiling, time-based metrics such as time to take-off, RSI-modified or flight time:contraction time for fatigue monitoring, and asymmetry and landing force for rehabilitation. Before calling a change real, compare it with the test's coefficient of variation: in the worked example a 2.9% jump height change was below a 3.8% CV and so was not counted as real.
paper.athleteDev: For profiling, jump height, peak force and peak power are reasonable choices because they relate to strength and speed. For fatigue monitoring, add time-based metrics, and check each athlete's own variability before reacting to a change.
paper.rtp: The review does not set return-to-sport criteria. It notes that asymmetries above 10% have been associated with injury risk in prior work and that peak power did not predict future injury in two cited studies, so a jump test alone should not decide return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Subjective wellness acute-chronic workloads and injury risk in college football.pdf

paper.citation: Sampson JA, Murray A, Williams S, Sullivan A, Fullagar HHK. Subjective wellness, acute:chronic workloads and injury risk in college football. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2019.
paper.abstract: In one season of data from 42 NCAA Division I football players, high and low daily EWMA ACWRs were associated with higher 3-day noncontact injury risk. High ACWRs were also trivially associated with lower self-reported wellness, and the highest-risk group was athletes who reported 'better' soreness on high-ACWR days.
paper.tldr: Both unusually high and unusually low workload ratios preceded more noncontact injuries in this college squad, so watching for load spikes and drops still makes sense. Self-reported wellness did not predict injury by itself, and a 'feeling good' report after a load spike is not a reason to add more load.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of one season of GPS and accelerometer workload (PlayerLoad) and a three-item daily wellness questionnaire from 42 athletes. Daily 7:21-day EWMA ACWRs were aligned with the next day's pre-training wellness, and a generalized linear mixed model with player as a random effect estimated 3-day noncontact injury risk, interpreted with magnitude-based probabilities.
paper.findings: Across 1,807 training-day records, 55 noncontact injuries occurred. Injury risk was very likely higher at ACWRs 2 SD above (RR 3.05) and 2 SD below (RR 2.49) the mean ACWR of 0.91. High ACWR combined with 'better' soreness was likely or very likely riskier than 'normal' soreness (RR 1.64, 90% CI 1.10 to 2.47) and than 'worse' soreness (RR 2.78, 90% CI 1.21 to 6.38). No clear interaction was found for sleep or energy, and no clear injury effect was found for 'better' or 'worse' wellness on its own.
paper.limitations: The study is one season from one team with 55 injuries, and the authors say the interaction analyses were likely underpowered. The overall-wellness interaction results (RR 1.52, 90% CI 0.91 to 2.54; RR 2.36, 90% CI 0.83 to 6.74) are labelled 'likely' higher risk under magnitude-based inference in both the abstract and results, although their 90% intervals include 1; the abstract also misprints the upper limit as 674. The authors suggest coaches or players may have changed load after poor wellness reports, so the results are associations, not causes. Absolute risks stayed below 15% even at the extremes.
paper.practicalImplications: Use EWMA ACWR together with a simple daily wellness check, and treat large swings in load as a reason to review the session plan. Because the highest-risk group was athletes who felt 'better' on high-ACWR days, do not use good self-reported soreness as a reason to add unplanned load. The authors' suggestion to avoid daily ACWR fluctuations of more than 1 SD of a player's average is practical guidance, not a tested threshold.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the study supports tracking the EWMA ACWR and short-term wellness together and checking planned against actual load before adding intensity. Sudden rises and sudden drops in load both warrant review, and athletes who feel fine after a spike still need the same check.
paper.rtp: This study cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. It examined workload and wellness in a healthy training season, and the discussion's mention of return to play as a high-ACWR scenario was not measured, so it should not be used to set return-to-play load limits.

records.sourceFile: Terminology and Interpretation Across Neuromuscular Profiling Methods - A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Chua KYH, Leahey SR, Lum D, Fahey JT, Buchheit M, Laffer JC, et al. Terminology and interpretation across neuromuscular profiling methods: a systematic review. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined whether the terms used to describe outputs from six neuromuscular profiling methods match what the methods measure. Across 184 included studies, terms such as 'explosive', 'springy', 'stiff' and 'strong/weak' were often applied without consistent definitions, and reliability was rarely reported.
paper.tldr: Neuromuscular profiling labels such as 'explosive', 'springy' and 'strong' are often inferred rather than measured, and the same metric is labelled differently across studies. Report the actual metric and its components, and do not treat a label as a validated athlete classification.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus (searched February 2023, updated to September 2024) for six profiling methods: DSI, EUR, RSI, RSImod, force-velocity profiling and impulse analysis. Two reviewers screened studies, 184 were included after full-text review, and extracted output values, terms, mechanisms and reliability data were grouped into four themes. Study quality was rated with a customised 10-item tool.
paper.findings: Reported DSI values ranged from 0.46 to 0.92, but common value ranges could not be set for EUR, RSI or RSImod, so those were grouped by magnitude only. Higher EUR was mostly read as more efficient stretch-shortening cycle function, but two studies read it the opposite way. For DSI, 'strong' or 'weak' labels were based on isometric peak force from the IMTP rather than on the DSI itself, and 'explosive' was inferred without measuring rate of force development; for RSI and RSImod, labels were a mix of measured and inferred. Only 47 of 184 sources (26%) reported reliability statistics.
paper.limitations: The synthesis is interpretive, with subjective coding of terms and the authors' own quality tool. The protocol was not pre-registered, the search was limited to English journal articles, and the EUR and RSI study groups scored only 'fair' on quality. Many RSI studies (33 of 72) did not report both constituent variables (jump height and contact time), which limits interpretation. Crossref lists 2026, but the PDF prints only 2025 on the copyright and accepted-date lines, so 2025 is kept.
paper.practicalImplications: Report the actual neuromuscular metric and its components, such as peak forces for DSI or jump height and contact time for RSI, rather than a single label. Avoid calling athletes 'explosive', 'springy' or 'stiff' unless the underlying measure supports it. Check whether a test has reliability data before acting on a change, and keep jump instructions and calculation methods the same within a team.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports choosing profiling methods that match the quality of interest rather than running all of them, and keeping their constituent variables in view when discussing an athlete's profile. Define the terms you use for coaches, and track change within the same test protocol so differences reflect the athlete rather than the method.
paper.rtp: This review included only healthy participants and does not study injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot set return-to-play criteria. Do not use these profiling labels to judge strength, stiffness or readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: The applicability of the risk score approach to competitive sport - Development of a physical success score for the Canadian Football League Combine.pdf

paper.citation: Matsuo H, Funasaki K, Yamada S. The applicability of the risk score approach to competitive sport: development of a physical success score for the Canadian Football League combine. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(3):695-701.
paper.abstract: The authors built a simple scoring system, the physical success score (PSS), from CFL Combine measures to classify draft success for three position groups. Cross-validated logistic models identified the predictors and reference values for each group.
paper.tldr: Position-specific score tables link combine measures such as height, mass and 40-yard sprint time to draft selection, and show the draft probability for each total score. Use them as reference points for goal setting, not as a prediction for any one player.
paper.methods: Combine data (40-yard dash, bench press, vertical jump, broad jump, shuttle run, 3-cone drill, height and mass) and binary draft outcome were taken from public CFL records for players in three position groups. Repeated grid-search cross-validation selected predictors for a logistic model, and each measure was scored by category against a base category, with draft probability estimated for every possible total score.
paper.findings: The final models included height, mass and 40-yard sprint in all groups, with vertical jump in the line group, 3-cone in the line and big skill groups, and bench press in the big skill and skill groups; only the 40-yard sprint was significant in all three models. Validation AUCs for the PSS were 0.77 (line), 0.76 (big skill) and 0.83 (skill), above the classification tree benchmark (0.71, 0.67 and 0.78). The score tables show, for example, a line total score of 2.0 corresponding to a draft probability of 79.5 to 90.5 percent.
paper.limitations: The outcome is drafted or not, regardless of round, so it does not measure playing success. The abstract gives 211 line players, while the Methods and Table 4 give 221, and the regression models used only 176, 141 and 185 players with complete data. The validation AUCs in the Methods (0.81, 0.79 and 0.88) differ from those in the Results (0.77, 0.76 and 0.83); the final score was taken from the best-performing validation fold, and the model was not tested on independent players. The authors describe the scores as reference values for size and athletic ability, not skill.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can use the position-specific tables to see which combine-style measures (height, mass, 40-yard sprint, and for some groups bench press or 3-cone) relate to draft selection, and what a total score implies. Use the tables as goal reference points and progress markers, since they describe past selections and exclude skill.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff working with gridiron prospects, the tables give position-specific targets for body size, 40-yard speed and strength or agility. The authors suggest the gaps between an athlete's results and the target bands can guide training priorities, while skill assessment has to be done separately because the scores do not measure it.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It relates combine-day test results to draft selection in prospects and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play.

records.sourceFile: The deceleration deficit - A novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance.pdf

paper.citation: Clarke R, Read PJ, De Ste Croix MBA, Hughes JD. The deceleration deficit: a novel field-based method to quantify deceleration during change of direction performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(9):2434-2439.
paper.abstract: The study compared a new field-based deceleration deficit (DD) with the established change-of-direction deficit (CODD) and linear sprint speed in 36 athletes. Linear speed was strongly related to 505 time but not to either deficit, while DD was moderately related to 505 time and more strongly to CODD.
paper.tldr: Linear sprint time and CODD both tracked 505 time closely in this sample, while the new deceleration deficit (DD) was only moderately related to it. DD may show braking ability that CODD hides, since the two disagree for most athletes, so check both, per turning direction, before deciding what limits an athlete.
paper.methods: In one session, 36 university-level invasion-sport athletes completed three 505 trials in each turning direction and three 15-m sprints with timing gates and a contact mat at the turn. DD was the 505 full-approach time (to mid plant-step contact) minus the 15-m sprint time, and CODD was the 505 time minus the 10-m sprint time. Pearson correlations and z-score differences against a moderate worthwhile change (0.5 x between-subject SD) compared the measures.
paper.findings: Linear sprint times correlated with 505 time (r = 0.71 to 0.76), while neither 10-m nor 15-m sprint time was related to CODD or DD. CODD correlated with 505 time (r = 0.74 to 0.77), and DD correlated with 505 time (r = 0.41 to 0.44), with full approach time (r = 0.43 to 0.54) and with CODD (r = 0.59 to 0.62). A moderate worthwhile change between the two deficit z-scores was seen in 78 percent of athletes (28 of 36) in at least one turning direction.
paper.limitations: The study is a single-session cross-sectional correlation with 36 athletes, and the authors state that the reliability and validity of DD still need testing; without reliability data, some of the DD versus CODD divergence may reflect measurement error. No force-plate data were collected, so the braking contribution cannot be measured directly. The paper describes the sample as both recreationally active and competitive university-level. The authors state that all DD correlations were below r = 0.5, but their tables show r = 0.59 to 0.62 with CODD and 0.54 with full approach in the nondominant direction, and the abstract's claim that linear speed has the strongest relationship with 505 time is not supported by the tables (CODD r = 0.74 to 0.77, full approach r = 0.86 to 0.87); table values are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the 505 test with a 15-m sprint in the same session to separate linear speed from braking ability, and compare DD with CODD for each turning direction. When the two deficits disagree, the paper suggests CODD alone could misjudge an athlete's deceleration, so look at DD before deciding whether deceleration is the limiter. Because the metric is not yet tested for reliability, use the flag to guide further assessment, not as a fixed training prescription.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the study supports testing linear speed and deceleration separately instead of relying on total 505 time or CODD alone. Look at both turning directions, since the paper shows the two deficits often disagree. Track how athletes respond to any deceleration-focused work, because the paper does not show that training DD changes change-of-direction performance.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested currently uninjured athletes in one session and did not assess injured athletes, rehabilitation or change in deceleration after injury. Do not use DD as a return-to-sport or change-of-direction clearance criterion.

records.sourceFile: The Reliability, Bias, Differences, and Agreement Between Velocity Measurement Devices During the Hang Clean Pull.pdf

paper.citation: Kissick CR, Techmanski BS, Comfort P, Suchomel TJ. The Reliability, Bias, Differences, and Agreement Between Velocity Measurement Devices During the Hang Clean Pull. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(3):289-294.
paper.abstract: This study compared the reliability, bias and agreement of two barbell velocity devices (GymAware PowerTool and Tendo Power Analyzer) during the hang clean pull in 14 resistance-trained men across loads from 20% to 140% of 1RM hang power clean. Both devices were reliable, but at 140% 1RM the Tendo showed proportional bias for mean and peak velocity and fixed bias for peak velocity. The authors conclude that the two devices are reliable and that differences between them are not practically meaningful, although the Tendo slightly overestimates velocity.
paper.tldr: Both velocity devices gave reliable barbell velocity data across hang clean pull loads up to 140% of 1RM. The Tendo overestimated velocity by a small amount and was less reliable for peak velocity at heavier loads, so the two devices should not be used interchangeably.
paper.methods: Fourteen resistance-trained men completed a 1RM hang power clean test and, one week later, three single hang clean pulls at each of 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120 and 140% of 1RM, with a GymAware PowerTool and a Tendo Power Analyzer attached to the barbell. Within-session reliability across repetitions was assessed with ICCs and typical error (CV%), with the GymAware as criterion; least-products regression and Hedges' g effect sizes assessed bias and differences between devices.
paper.findings: The authors describe GymAware reliability as excellent for all mean (ICC 0.94 to 0.97) and peak (ICC 0.88 to 0.95) barbell velocity measures. The Tendo was excellent for mean velocity at all loads and for peak velocity at 20 to 80% 1RM, good at 100 and 120%, and moderate at 140% (ICC 0.73). The Tendo overestimated mean velocity by 3.7 to 6.8% and peak velocity by 1.8 to 2.9%, and proportional bias (mean and peak velocity) and fixed bias (peak velocity) appeared only at 140% 1RM. Between-device effect sizes were small (MBV g = 0.35 to 0.57; PBV g = 0.23 to 0.54) and were not classed as practically meaningful.
paper.limitations: The GymAware was used as the criterion device, not 3D motion capture, so the accuracy of both devices against a gold standard is not established. The sample was 14 resistance-trained men, and the authors say results may not generalize to other populations. Comparable hang clean pull data are limited, and the Tendo's peak velocity reliability declined at heavier loads. The text calls all GymAware values excellent, but Table 1 shows a peak velocity ICC of 0.88 at 120% 1RM, which is good by the authors' own cut-offs.
paper.practicalImplications: Either device can give reliable mean and peak barbell velocity during hang clean pulls at loads from 20% to 140% of 1RM hang power clean. The Tendo became less reliable for peak velocity at heavier loads, possibly because it does not correct for horizontal bar movement, so practitioners should read its heavy-load peak velocity values with caution. The authors say the Tendo's small overestimation can be accounted for if the same device is used consistently.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches using velocity to load hang clean pulls can use either device for monitoring at up to 140% of 1RM hang power clean, but should use one device consistently so that values can be compared over time. Peak velocity from the Tendo at heavy loads should be interpreted with caution.
paper.rtp: The study tested resistance-trained men in a lab and included no injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or criteria.

records.sourceFile: The Role of Speed, Change of Direction, and Momentum by Position and Starting Status in Division 1 Collegiate Football Players.pdf

paper.citation: Mann JB, Cowley N, Weakley J. The Role of Speed, Change of Direction, and Momentum by Position and Starting Status in Division 1 Collegiate Football Players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(1):41-47.
paper.abstract: This study analyzed 15 years of 40-yard sprint, pro-agility and L drill data from 496 Division 1 football players to compare positional groups and starters with nonstarters. Positions differed in speed and momentum, and starters were faster and had greater momentum than nonstarters. The authors found no practically useful ROC thresholds for separating starters from nonstarters, and they advise against binary selection thresholds.
paper.tldr: In Division 1 football, positional groups differed in sprint, change of direction and momentum, and starters outperformed nonstarters by small to moderate margins. Cutoffs built from these tests were poor at identifying starters, so the tests should guide development and profiling, not selection.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of performance data from 496 first-year NCAA Division 1 football athletes across 15 years. Athletes were grouped as big, mid or skill position and as starter or nonstarter. Each athlete completed the 40-yard sprint, pro-agility and L drill, with momentum calculated from body mass and average velocity. Linear mixed models compared groups, and ROC curves set cutoffs for starter status.
paper.findings: Positional groups differed significantly on all tests, with moderate to very large effects. Starters were faster than nonstarters within each positional group (for example, 40-yard sprint 5.18 vs 5.30 s in big positions, 4.70 vs 4.87 s in mid, and 4.52 vs 4.69 s in skill), with small to moderate effects, and had greater momentum. ROC curves gave AUC values of 0.57 to 0.76 (poor to fair), with sensitivity up to 94% but positive predictive values of 15% to 43%.
paper.limitations: The data come from a single program under one head coach, so playing style and selection practices may have shaped the results. Starter status was the only outcome, and binary ROC models had poor to fair discrimination. The authors suggest that multivariable methods and larger datasets would be needed to build better selection tools. Pro-agility and L drill were hand-timed with stopwatches, and tests came from the first year while starter status counted any start across the career. Table 5 labels an AUC of 0.57 as fair, although the stated cut-offs class it as poor.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches should profile positions using different measures: emphasize absolute sprint and change of direction time for skill players, and monitor momentum for big players. The authors advise against using these tests with fixed thresholds to select or cut players, since the ROC cutoffs had low positive predictive value. Speed, change of direction and momentum should be developed alongside technical and tactical ability.
paper.athleteDev: The authors recommend using the position profile to set development priorities: skill players build absolute speed and change of direction, big players ensure enough body mass to create momentum, and mid players balance both. These are recommendations from cross-sectional data, and the paper advises developing these qualities rather than using them as a selection tool.
paper.rtp: The study does not include injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes, and it offers no return-to-play thresholds. The tests describe general performance by position, so they cannot be used to decide whether an athlete is ready to return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp.pdf

paper.citation: Smith-Hale V, Mendoza R, Vargo C, Schoen M, Jimenez L, VanSumeren M, et al. Training Impulse and Session Ratings of Perceived Exertion as Perceived by Athletes and Observed by Coaches During Preseason Football Camp. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025.
paper.abstract: Compared heart-rate training impulse with session RPE load from athletes, a football coach and a strength and conditioning coach during the first six practices of preseason camp in collegiate American football players, and examined first-year versus returning athletes and heart-rate recovery measures.
paper.tldr: In one Division II football team's first six camp practices, athlete and coach ratings of session load tracked heart-rate load only moderately. Use ratings alongside heart-rate data, not as a substitute for it.
paper.methods: Prospective study during the first six official practices of preseason camp; 29 athletes enrolled and 5 were excluded for missing 2 or more practices. Athletes wore chest-strap heart-rate monitors to calculate TRIMP and rated each session on the CR10 session RPE scale; the football and strength and conditioning coaches rated each athlete. Heart rate variability and resting heart rate were measured before practice. Pearson correlations and Mann-Whitney U tests were used.
paper.findings: Across 139 observations, session loads correlated significantly with Edwards TRIMP: athletes r = 0.62, football coach r = 0.68 and strength and conditioning coach r = 0.49. Correlations were stronger in first-year athletes (0.68, 0.79, 0.64) than returning athletes (0.60, 0.70, 0.40). First-year athletes had a higher heart-rate load than returning athletes (median 780 vs 697), lower HRV and higher resting heart rate, but their own ratings did not differ (median 780 vs 735); the strength coach rated first-year athletes higher and the football coach rated them lower than returning players. HRV was inversely related to load (r = -0.29 for Edwards TRIMP) and resting heart rate positively related (r = 0.22), both small.
paper.limitations: Small, unbalanced sample of 24 athletes and 2 coaches from one team over six practices, with maximal heart rate estimated for most athletes. The strength coach correlation is 0.49 in the abstract and results but 0.41 in the Discussion, and the Discussion's R2 of 0.17 matches 0.41, not 0.49. Figure 2 reports N = 129 observations versus 139 in the text, the Figure 3 caption reverses the group sizes, and Table 1 gives a combined body fat (29.96%) higher than both group means (30.82% and 25.6%), which is not possible. Results tables and text values were used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Ratings and heart-rate load agree only moderately, so session RPE from athletes or coaches should not be treated as interchangeable with heart-rate monitoring. The authors suggest both kinds of measure add unique information and that feedback on heart rate may help coaches and athletes align their ratings, which this study did not test.
paper.athleteDev: During preseason camp, athlete and football coach ratings tracked heart-rate load with low-to-moderate agreement. The single strength and conditioning coach, who had under one year with the program, agreed least, so the authors suggest strength staff need better information on cumulative field-practice load; this cannot be generalized beyond these two coaches.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It examined collegiate athletes in preseason practice and did not study injured or returning athletes or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives - Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons.pdf

paper.citation: Suchomel TJ, Kissick CR, Techmanski BS, Mann JB, Comfort P. Velocity-Based Training With Weightlifting Derivatives: Barbell and System Velocity Comparisons. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2025;39(2):135-146.
paper.abstract: Compared mean and peak barbell velocity with system velocity (athlete plus load) during five weightlifting derivatives across a range of relative loads in 14 resistance-trained men, using force platforms and linear position transducers.
paper.tldr: In resistance-trained men, barbell velocity was consistently and substantially higher than system velocity across five weightlifting pulls and every load tested. Treat the two as different measures and do not swap one for the other.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures design. Participants completed six sessions over about two weeks, starting with a 1RM hang power clean test, then one session per exercise in randomized order. Three individual repetitions were performed at each load: 20% to 100% (jump shrug and hang high pull), 20% to 80% (hang power clean), and 20% to 140% (hang clean pull and countermovement shrug) of hang power clean 1RM. Barbell velocity came from a linear position transducer and system velocity from force-platform integration; reliability used ICC and CV, and differences used repeated-measures ANOVA and Hedges g.
paper.findings: Mean and peak barbell velocity exceeded system velocity at every exercise and load (p < 0.001, Hedges g 1.49 to 6.73). For example, the hang power clean at 20% gave mean barbell velocity 1.46 m/s against mean system velocity 0.62 m/s. All mean system velocities were below 1.00 m/s except the jump shrug at 20% to 60%. ICCs ranged from 0.77 to 0.99, and all CVs were under 10% except mean system velocity for the jump shrug at 20% (11.7%).
paper.limitations: Individual repetitions rather than sets, some loads lighter than typical prescription, and a small sample of resistance-trained men who were not competitive weightlifters. Reliability was lowest at light loads (for example, peak system velocity ICC 0.77 to 0.79 at 20% for the countermovement shrug and hang clean pull). The authors note that subject height and limb length may affect barbell velocity, and call for research across sets and populations.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not interpret barbell velocity readings from a bar-mounted device as body or system velocity during weightlifting pulls. The authors recommend using peak rather than mean velocity to characterize these exercises, because the transition phase may limit what mean velocity says about load; this recommendation was not directly tested.
paper.athleteDev: Barbell and system velocity give different numbers for the same lift, so velocity targets for pulling derivatives should state which one they use. The authors suggest barbell velocity matters most for weightlifters and system velocity for non-weightlifters, and that the jump shrug suits velocity emphasis and the countermovement shrug force emphasis, based on the velocity profiles here.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested individual repetitions of pulling lifts in a lab with healthy resistance-trained men and did not include injured athletes or return-to-play testing.
